front: What is the fundamental value F_t in Definition 1.2?
back: The present value at date t of the dividends paid after t: F_t = sum over k of d_(t+k) / (1 + r)^k, for k from 1 to infinity, whenever the series converges. It is a benchmark computed from dividends and the discount rate, not a forecast of any price.

front: Theorem 1.3 (closed form). Hypotheses: A0, r > g and 1 + g > 0; A1, d_s = d_1 (1 + g)^(s-1) for every s >= 1, with d_1 real. What is F_t for every integer t >= 0?
back: F_t = d_1 (1 + g)^t / (r - g) = d_(t+1) / (r - g). In particular F_0 = d_1 / (r - g).

front: Theorem 1.3 with hypotheses A0 (r > g, 1 + g > 0) and A1 (d_s = d_1 (1 + g)^(s-1)). What identity do the partial sums S_N(t) satisfy, for every N >= 1?
back: S_N(t) = F_t (1 - q^N) exactly, for every N >= 1, with q = (1 + g) / (1 + r).
basis: Proof in Section 1 (Theorem 1.3); Lab 1 Part A (exact check, t = 0)

front: Under A0 (r > g and 1 + g > 0), what range does q = (1 + g) / (1 + r) lie in, and what follows for the partial sums?
back: 0 < q < 1. So q^N tends to 0, and the partial sums converge to F_t.

front: Proposition 1.4 (no finite benchmark). Hypotheses: (A1) d_s = d_1 (1 + g)^(s-1) with d_1 > 0 and 1 + g > 0, and (A2) r > -1 and g >= r. What happens to the partial sums S_N(0) as N grows?
back: S_N(0) tends to +infinity. The series in Definition 1.2 does not converge, so Theorem 1.3 does not apply.

front: Definition 2.1: what is the speculative bubble at date t, relative to the benchmark F_t?
back: The gap B_t = A_t - F_t, counted as a bubble only when B_t > 0. The gap is measured in cents. A price with B_t <= 0 has no bubble on this definition.

front: Proposition 2.2. Hypotheses: (A3) d_1 > 0; (A4) Assumption 1.1 holds with growth rates g < g' and one discount rate r, where r > g, r > g', 1 + g > 0 and 1 + g' > 0. What is the ordering of F_0(g) and F_0(g')?
Definition 3.1: how is a financial panic defined?
back: A sudden, collective demand by holders of financial claims to convert them into money or into assets regarded as safe, in which many claims fall in price together or trading in them stops. The definition names the mechanism only. It states no frequency, trigger or size.

front: Lab 1 Part B (SIMULATED): under the stated 3 percent growth, in how many of the 13 periods t = 0 to 12 is the price above the fundamental?
back: 9 of 13. This is one seeded draw of the wedges, not an estimate for any market.

front: Lab 1 Part C (SIMULATED): with the same prices and 1 percent growth, in how many of the 13 periods is the price above the alternative fundamental?
back: 13 of 13. The count changes with the assumed growth rate, from 9 of 13 under 3 percent.

front: Is a price above the present value of the dividends a bubble?
back: Only relative to the stated benchmark. With d_1 = 400 cents and r = 9 percent, a price of 6000 cents is above the benchmark under 1 percent growth and below it under 3 percent growth (Proposition 2.2).

front: Does d_1 / (r - g) give the present value of any dividend stream?
back: No. The formula needs (A1), which fixes every dividend from d_1 and g. A stream with d_1 = 400 cents, d_2 = 0, d_s = 0 for every s >= 3, and r = 9 percent has present value 40000/109 cents, which is 367 cents to the nearest cent.
basis: Calculation in the canon-breaks list of L01 Section 5; Theorem 1.3 proof uses (A1)

front: Under (A1) with d_1 > 0 and 1 + g > 0, and (A2) r > -1 and g >= r, what lower bound does each discounted dividend d_k / (1 + r)^k satisfy for every k >= 1?
back: Each term is at least d_1 / (1 + r), which is positive.

front: Definition 1.1: what does a gold standard fix?
back: A parity kappa > 0, the quantity of gold in grams for one unit of the currency.

front: Proposition 1.2. Hypothesis (A1): the issuer keeps the parity kappa at every date t. What does one gram of gold cost at date t?
back: 1/kappa units of the currency, at every date t.

front: Does fixing the gold price of the currency fix the price level?
back: No. Proposition 1.2 gives one price, the currency price of gold. Its hypothesis (A1), the parity kept at every date, does not involve the price index P_t of Section 2, so its conclusion holds whatever path P_t follows.

front: What is the real value V_t of a fixed nominal debt D, in base-date cents?
back: V_t = D P_0 / P_t, where D is the nominal amount in integer cents and P_0 is the base value of the price index.

front: Proposition 2.1, part (a). Hypotheses: (A2) D is a fixed positive integer number of cents, paid in full and not renegotiated; (A3) P_t is a positive real number for every date t. What is V_t / V_(t-1) for t >= 1?
back: P_(t-1) / P_t. The factor D P_0 cancels in the ratio.

front: Proposition 2.1, part (b). Hypotheses: (A2) D is a fixed positive integer number of cents, paid in full and not renegotiated; (A3) P_t is positive for every date t. What is V_H / V_0 for every H >= 1?
back: P_0 / P_H. The one-period ratios of part (a) telescope.

front: Definition 3.1: what is debt deflation?
back: The rise in the real value V_t of a fixed nominal debt that a fall in the price index P_t implies by the identity of Proposition 2.1, with D held fixed. It is an arithmetic consequence, not a claim about the cause of any fall.

front: Corollary 3.2. Hypotheses: (A2) and (A3) of Proposition 2.1. For t >= 1, when does the real value rise, V_t > V_(t-1)?
back: If and only if P_t < P_(t-1), so the real value rises exactly in the periods in which the index falls.

front: Proposition 2.1 has hypotheses (A2) and (A3) only. Does its conclusion depend on the path that the price index P_t follows?
back: No. Proposition 2.1 holds for every index path that satisfies (A3), whatever the movements of the index and whatever caused them (Remark 2.2).

front: Under (A2) and (A3) of Proposition 2.1, when prices fall, does a fixed nominal debt become cheaper to repay?
back: No. Corollary 3.2 gives the opposite direction for the real value: a fall in P_t raises V_t, so the same nominal payment is a larger real burden.

front: Is the real value of a fixed nominal debt constant over time?
back: Not in general. V_t = D P_0 / P_t is constant exactly when P_t is constant, and it changes whenever P_t changes.
basis: Section 2 identity V_t = D P_0 / P_t; misconception 3 (Section 5)

front: Lab 1 (SIMULATED): on the simulated path, does the identity V_t / V_(t-1) = P_(t-1) / P_t hold at every date from 1 to 12?
back: Yes. It holds exactly at all 12 dates, as Lab 1 Part B prints.
basis: Lab 1 Part B (SIMULATED, one seeded path)

front: Assumption 1.1 (parity and deflation). What is the model's price index P_t, and what happens after period m?
back: P_t = (1 - delta)^min(t, m), with P_0 = 1, for 0 <= m <= H and 0 < delta < 1. The index falls by the fraction delta in each period on parity and is flat after period m.

front: Definition 2.1: what is leverage L_t in the model?
back: The ratio L_t = V_t / K_t of the real debt V_t to the borrower's net worth K_t.

front: In the model, what is the external-finance premium psi_t?
back: The rise in the extra cost of outside funds above its baseline: psi_t = phi (L_t - L_0), with slope phi > 0 (Assumption 1.3).

front: State the credit channel of a depression, as the model's chain (Definition 2.2).
back: A fall in the price index raises the real value of the fixed nominal debt (A1 and A2). The rise lowers borrower net worth one for one (A2). Higher leverage raises the premium (A3). The premium lowers output by f_t = beta psi_t, a fraction of baseline output, with output coefficient beta > 0 (A3). The chain describes the model and no economy outside it.

front: Lemma 3.1. Hypotheses: Assumptions 1.1 and 1.2, so that K_0 > 0; C = K_0 + D; for D <= x < C, lambda(x) = x / (C - x). What does L_t equal?
back: L_t = lambda(V_t) whenever V_t < C, and L_0 = D / K_0.

front: Proposition 3.2(a). Hypotheses: Assumptions 1.1 to 1.3, including the inequality V_m < K_0 + D of Assumption 1.2, with V_m = D (1 - delta)^(-m). What bound holds for the real debt over the horizon?
back: V_t <= V_m for every t from 0 to H.

front: Proposition 3.2(b). Hypotheses: Assumptions 1.1 to 1.3. What is depth(m) in closed form?
back: depth(m) = beta phi (lambda(V_m) - lambda(D)) = beta phi (V_m / (K_0 + D - V_m) - D / K_0), with V_m = D (1 - delta)^(-m).

front: Proposition 3.2(c). Hypotheses: Assumptions 1.1 to 1.3. In which period is the maximum of the output fall first attained?
back: At t = m. When m >= 1, no earlier period attains the maximum.

front: Under Assumptions 1.1 to 1.3, what is depth(0)?
back: Zero. With m = 0, P_t = 1 for every t, so V_t = D, L_t = L_0 and the premium is zero in every period.

front: Corollary 3.3. Hypotheses: Assumptions 1.1 to 1.3 for two economies that share D, K_0, delta, phi and beta, with parity durations m' and m and 0 <= m' < m <= H. What is the ordering of depth(m') and depth(m)?
back: depth(m') < depth(m): under these assumptions, the model economy with the longer parity duration has the strictly deeper fall. In Lab 1 (SIMULATED), economy X (m = 12) is therefore deeper than economy Y (m' = 4).

front: Corollary 3.4. Hypotheses: Assumptions 1.1 to 1.3 for two economies that share D, K_0, delta, phi and beta, with parity durations m' and m and 1 <= m' < m <= H. What is depth(m) / depth(m')?
back: (lambda(V_m) - lambda(D)) / (lambda(V_m') - lambda(D)). The right-hand side does not depend on beta or phi.

front: Lab 1 Part B (SIMULATED, phi = beta = 1): what is economy X's output depth, as a percent of baseline output?
back: 9.20 percent of baseline output.
basis: Lab 1, Part B (SIMULATED model values, printed to two decimals)

front: Lab 1 Part B (SIMULATED, phi = beta = 1): what is economy Y's output depth, as a percent of baseline output?
back: 2.69 percent of baseline output.
basis: Lab 1, Part B (SIMULATED model values, printed to two decimals)

front: Lab 1 Part D (SIMULATED): what is the ratio of the depth of X to the depth of Y for beta phi = 1, to four decimals?
Definition 4.1: what is a lender of last resort?
back: A central bank that lends against collateral to institutions that are solvent but illiquid.

front: Definition 4.1: what does it mean for an institution to be illiquid?
back: The institution cannot meet its payments from its own resources in the time available.

front: Under Assumptions 1.1 to 1.3, does Proposition 3.2 say what a lender of last resort does to the premium?
back: No. Assumption 1.2 has no lending term, and Assumption 1.3 has no term through which a facility changes the premium of a solvent borrower. The proposition therefore says nothing about a facility.

front: Does the model show that bank failures caused the depth?
back: No. The model has one borrower and no bank (misconception 1, Section 6). Assumption 1.2 excludes default and any other change to the balance sheet, so no failure occurs. The proof of Proposition 3.2 uses none of these events.
basis: Assumption 1.2 and the proof of Proposition 3.2

front: Does economy X's larger depth show that holding parity makes output fall further?
back: No. The ordering follows from the parity durations of 12 and 4 that Lab 1 assigns to economies X and Y under Assumption 1.1. The model cannot say whether holding parity causes a deeper fall.
basis: Proof of Corollary 3.3; Lab 1 Part B

front: Is it correct that a lender of last resort lends to any firm that asks, so that panics end?
back: No. Definition 4.1 requires collateral and limits lending to institutions that are solvent but illiquid. The model has no lending facility, so no panic result follows from it (Remark 4.2).

front: Is the 9.20 percent depth in Lab 1 a measured fall in output?
back: No. It is a SIMULATED model value under Assumption 1.3 with phi = beta = 1, and no output series enters the lab. Changing beta changes the depth in proportion, through the factor beta phi (Proposition 3.2(b)).

front: Does the L03 lab use an embedded historical series for gold-standard adherence or for output depth?
back: No. No redistributable historical series for either quantity is embedded, so the lab runs the stylised model and is labelled SIMULATED.

front: Definition 1.1: what is the monthly log change at month t?
back: ell_t = ln(x_t / x_(t-1)), the natural logarithm of the ratio of two consecutive rates. It is a change per month and is not annualized.

front: What is the dispersion of a window of monthly log changes?
back: The sample standard deviation of the n changes, with denominator n - 1, about their mean.

front: Proposition 1.2 (telescoping). Assuming (A1): the rates x_t are positive for every month from a to b, with a < b. What is the sum of ell_t for t from a + 1 to b?
back: ln(x_b / x_a). The sum has b - a terms.

front: Is Lab 1's check of Proposition 1.2 an exact check in floating-point arithmetic?
back: No. Proposition 1.2 is an exact identity in real numbers. The lab checks it in floating point to a tolerance of 10^-12, which confirms the computation to that tolerance only.
basis: Remark 1.3; the tolerance SUM_TOLERANCE = 1e-12 in the Lab 1 code

front: Proposition 2.2 (zero dispersion in the model). Hypotheses: (A2) for the model of Definition 2.1, with \(\bar{x} > 0\) and a window of at least two monthly changes, so that \(x_t = \bar{x}\) at the month before the window's first change and at every later month of the window. What are the monthly log changes and the dispersion of the window?
back: Every monthly log change is 0, and the dispersion is 0.

front: In L04, what does Definition 2.1 contain?
back: An anchor currency, in which every rate is quoted; one foreign currency; a fixed exchange rate \(\bar{x} > 0\), the number of anchor units per unit of the foreign currency; and a market rate \(x_t > 0\) at each month, in the same units.

front: Lab 1 Part B (embedded GBP column, all 668 monthly changes from 1971-02 to 2026-09): which months have an exactly zero monthly change?
basis: Lab 1 Part B (fx_monthly, MANIFEST retrieved 2026-10-19; GBP column)

front: Lab 1 Part C: what is the dispersion of window one, 1971-02 to 2026-09?
back: 0.027935 per month, from 668 monthly log changes (sample standard deviation with denominator 667).
basis: Lab 1 Part C (fx_monthly, MANIFEST retrieved 2026-10-19; GBP column)

front: Lab 1 Part C: what is the dispersion of window two, 2000-01 to 2026-09?
back: 0.024700 per month, from 321 monthly log changes.
basis: Lab 1 Part C (fx_monthly, MANIFEST retrieved 2026-10-19; GBP column)

front: Lab 1 Part D: what is window two's dispersion as a multiple of window one's?
back: 0.8842 times window one, to four decimals.
basis: Lab 1 Part D (fx_monthly, MANIFEST retrieved 2026-10-19; GBP column)

front: Lab 1 Part C: what is the largest absolute monthly log change in window two, and in which month?
back: 0.096575 in absolute value, at 2008-10.
basis: Lab 1 Part C (fx_monthly, MANIFEST retrieved 2026-10-19; GBP column)

front: Does a currency with a fixed exchange rate have no monthly change in its recorded rate?
back: Not necessarily. Proposition 2.2 gives zero change in the model under (A2), the rate held at \(\bar{x}\) from the month before the window's first change to its last change. (A2) describes the model, not a recorded rate, which need not equal \(\bar{x}\) at any month (Remark 2.3).

front: Does a smaller dispersion in window two show that the currency became calmer because of a regime change?
back: No. Lab 1 computes two sample standard deviations and their difference. It computes no test and names no cause, and the window start is a convention.
basis: Lab 1 Part D (fx_monthly, MANIFEST retrieved 2026-10-19; GBP column); L04 Problem E3 (the code contains no test)

front: Is the monthly log change the same number as the simple percent change?
back: No. A rise from 1.00 to 1.10 has a simple change of 0.10 and a log change of ln 1.1 = 0.095310 to six decimals, a difference of 0.004690.

front: Does the fixed-exchange-rate model of Definition 2.1 state what the historical Bretton Woods arrangement was?
back: No. Definition 2.1 defines a model class, not the historical arrangement. L04 gives no definition of the historical Bretton Woods system, and it states no historical fact about its fixed exchange rates, participants or end. Section 4 lists what is left open.

front: Why does window two start at 2000-01 in Lab 1?
back: It is the first month from which the other two embedded snapshots, fx_daily and ust_daily, have data, since both begin on 2000-01-03.

front: Which embedded dataset does Lab 1 read for its GBP column?
back: fx_monthly.csv: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, G.5/H.10 Foreign Exchange Rates (noon buying rates in New York), column GBP in US dollars per pound.

front: Lab 1 Part D: what is window two's dispersion minus window one's?
back: -0.003236. It is computed from the unrounded standard deviations, as Section 3 states.
basis: Lab 1 Part D (fx_monthly, MANIFEST retrieved 2026-10-19; GBP column)

front: Lab 1 (SIMULATED): on the simulated path, do the periods with a falling price index coincide with the periods with a rising real value?
back: Yes. Six of the twelve periods have a falling index and a rising real value, and the two sets of periods are equal.
basis: Lab 1 Part C (SIMULATED, one seeded path)

front: Lab 1 Part D (SIMULATED): does the ratio of the depths of X to Y change across the products beta phi = 1/2, 1 and 3?
back: No. Part D prints the same ratio for each product, as Corollary 3.4 implies, so the printed ratio does not change with beta phi.

front: Lab 1 Part B (embedded GBP column): how many monthly log changes in window one are nonzero?
back: 665 of the 668 changes are nonzero.
basis: Lab 1 Part B (fx_monthly, MANIFEST retrieved 2026-10-19; GBP column)

front: Does the embedded fx_monthly.csv hold any interest-rate or forward-rate column?
back: No. It holds exchange-rate columns only, so the lab cannot test a relation between interest rates and exchange rates.

front: In the model, how is borrower net worth K_t defined?
back: K_t = K_0 - (V_t - V_0), with K_0 the baseline net worth in cents. The whole rise in the real debt falls on net worth (Assumption 1.2).

front: In the model, how is the depth for parity duration m defined?
back: depth(m) = the maximum over 0 <= t <= H of f_t, where f_t = beta psi_t is the fall in output as a fraction of baseline output (Assumption 1.3).

front: In L02 Section 2, what is a nominal debt?
back: An amount of currency that the debtor owes at each date of a contract, stated in the currency's own units and not indexed to prices. Here the amount is D cents.

front: In L02 Section 2, what is the price index P_t, and what is its base value?
back: The index P_t at date t, with base date 0. Its values are positive numbers, and P_0 is the base value.

front: Definition 4.1: what does it mean for an institution to be solvent?
back: Its assets, valued as the lender values them, cover its liabilities.

front: Definition 1.1: what does convertibility at the parity require?
back: The issuer stands ready to buy and sell gold at the parity on demand.

front: Proposition 3.2(a), the real-debt path. Hypotheses: Assumptions 1.1 to 1.3, with V_m = D (1 - delta)^(-m). What is V_t for t at most m, and how does it behave when m >= 1?
back: V_t = D (1 - delta)^(-t) for t at most m, which is strictly increasing in t when m >= 1. For t at least m, V_t = V_m.

front: Definition 4.1: what is a central bank?
back: The public institution that issues the currency.

front: In Lab 1 Part B (SIMULATED), does the real value of the fixed nominal debt differ from its predecessor in each of the 12 periods?
back: Yes. Part B prints a real value that differs from the previous period's in every one of the twelve periods, so no period has an unchanged real value.
basis: Lab 1 Part B (SIMULATED, one seeded path)

front: Assumption 1.2: which inequality keeps borrower net worth positive in every period, and why?
back: V_m = D (1 - delta)^(-m) < K_0 + D. Proposition 3.2(a) gives V_t <= V_m for every t, so V_t < K_0 + D and K_t > 0 in every period (Remark 4.2).

front: In L04, what is a fixed-exchange-rate model, as Definition 2.1 defines it?
back: The model of Definition 2.1 together with Assumption (A2), fixed rate held: at every month from the month before the window's first change to its last change, \(x_t = \bar{x}\). It says nothing about a recorded rate (Remark 2.3).

front: How is each monthly value of the GBP column in fx_monthly.csv formed?
back: It is the column's last value in its month, a month-end value, as the MANIFEST transform states. It is not the monthly average that the Board publishes in its own monthly series.

front: Under Assumption 1.1, how is F_t related to F_(t-1) for t >= 1?
back: F_t = (1 + g) F_(t-1): the benchmark grows at the dividend growth rate g from one date to the next.

front: In the proof of Proposition 2.2, why does (A3), d_1 > 0, let the ordering F_0(g) < F_0(g') follow?
back: Both benchmarks are d_1 times a reciprocal. With r - g > r - g' > 0, the reciprocal 1/(r - g) is smaller than 1/(r - g'), and multiplying by the positive d_1 keeps that order.

front: Lemma 3.1, under Assumptions 1.1 and 1.2 with C = K_0 + D. Is lambda strictly increasing on [D, C)?
back: Yes. For D <= x < y < C, lambda(y) - lambda(x) = C (y - x) / ((C - x)(C - y)), which is positive.

front: For a window of monthly log changes, when is the dispersion defined?
back: Only when the window holds n >= 2 monthly log changes, because the denominator is n - 1.

front: Lab 1 Part C: what is the largest absolute monthly log change in window one, and in which month?
back: 0.135846 in absolute value, at 1985-03; the signed value is also 0.135846.
basis: Lab 1 Part C (fx_monthly, MANIFEST retrieved 2026-10-19; GBP column)

front: Lab 1 Part B (SIMULATED, phi = beta = 1): in which period is economy X's output depth first reached?
back: t = 12, the last of its 12 periods on parity (Proposition 3.2(c) places the first maximising period at t = m).
basis: Lab 1, Part B (SIMULATED model values); Proposition 3.2(c)

front: Lab 1 Part B (SIMULATED, phi = beta = 1): in which period is economy Y's output depth first reached?
back: t = 4, the last of its 4 periods on parity (Proposition 3.2(c) places the first maximising period at t = m).
basis: Lab 1, Part B (SIMULATED model values); Proposition 3.2(c)

front: With d_1 > 0 and g >= r, what does the closed form d_1/(r - g) give as the present value of the dividends?
back: No present value. At g = r the closed form is undefined, and at g > r it returns a negative number that is not the present value of the dividends. With d_1 = 400 cents, r = 9% and g = 10%, it gives 400/(0.09 - 0.10) = -40000 cents.

front: Proposition 2.2 hypotheses: (A3) d_1 > 0, and (A4) Assumption 1.1 with growth rates g < g' and one discount rate r, where r > g, r > g', 1 + g > 0 and 1 + g' > 0. For which prices A_0 is the gap positive under g and non-positive under g'?
back: Every price A_0 with F_0(g) < A_0 <= F_0(g'). For such a price the gap under g, A_0 - F_0(g), is positive, and the gap under g', A_0 - F_0(g'), is non-positive.
